outputs.L1:
**LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN)** — A group of Nigerian rebels that wrote to U.S. President George W. Bush, claiming responsibility for attacks on two oil pipelines Monday, has asked former President Jimmy Carter and actor George Clooney to help resolve issues in the oil-rich Niger Delta.

Military police patrol the creeks of the Omadino community in the Warri South district of the Niger Delta.

In the letter, the Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta, or MEND, said it had attacked two pipelines it believed were owned by Chevron Corp. and Shell Oil.

A spokesman for Royal Dutch Shell said the company’s pipeline was damaged last week. The attack will temporarily reduce shipments by 169,000 barrels a day while workers repair the damage, he said. The pipeline is jointly owned by Shell and Nigerian, French, and Italian oil companies.

Chevron spokesman Kurt Glaubitz told CNN, “No Chevron pipelines have been vandalized in Nigeria.”

There was no immediate comment from the Nigerian government.

In the letter, members of the group described themselves as “commandos” and said their aim was “the crippling of the Nigerian oil export industry.”

**Watch how attacks in Nigeria are helping drive up gas prices »**

“Today’s attack was prompted by the continuous injustice in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, where the root issues have not been addressed by the illegal and insincere government,” the letter stated.

The group said two other letters had been sent—to Bush and to actor George Clooney—and also asked former President Jimmy Carter to help.

Clooney is one of the United Nations’ Messengers of Peace and has campaigned for an end to the long-standing conflict in Darfur, as well as for expanded humanitarian relief efforts in the region.

Carter is currently in the Middle East, where he has met with exiled Hamas militant leader Khalid Meshaal as part of what he calls a “study mission” to support peace, democracy, and human rights in the region.

“MEND is prepared for talks and will prefer Ex President Jimmy Carter to mediate. Mr. Carter is not in denial as the rest of you who brand freedom fighters as terrorists,” the letter stated.

“The ripple effect of this attack will touch your economy and people one way or the other and hope we now have your attention.”

The organization also said the attack was carried out in response to the arrest of one of its members, Henry Okah, who was detained last year and, according to local reports, has been charged with treason.

Since late 2005, MEND militants have carried out numerous attacks on Nigeria’s oil sector and abducted dozens of foreign workers, nearly all of whom were released unharmed.

The organization has previously said it intensified its attacks to address what it describes as the unequal distribution of the nation’s oil wealth.

outputs.L2:
LAGOS, Nigeria (CNN) — Nigerian rebel organization the Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta (MEND) said in a letter to U.S. President George W. Bush that it attacked two oil pipelines on Monday. The group also requested help from former President Jimmy Carter and actor George Clooney in addressing problems in Nigeria’s oil-producing Niger Delta.

Military police officers were patrolling waterways near the Omadino community in the Warri South district of the Niger Delta.

MEND said the targeted pipelines were believed to belong to Chevron Corp. and Shell. A Royal Dutch Shell representative confirmed that a Shell pipeline had been damaged the previous week. According to the spokesman, repairs would temporarily reduce oil shipments by 169,000 barrels per day. He added that the pipeline is jointly owned by Shell and Nigerian, French, and Italian petroleum companies.

Chevron representative Kurt Glaubitz told CNN, “No Chevron pipelines have been vandalized in Nigeria.” Nigerian authorities did not immediately respond.

Describing its members as “commandos,” MEND said its objective was “the crippling of the Nigerian oil export industry.” The group claimed the assault resulted from continuing unfairness in the Niger Delta and accused what it called Nigeria’s “illegal and insincere government” of failing to resolve the region’s underlying problems.

MEND said two additional letters had been sent to Bush and Clooney, and it asked Carter to become involved. Clooney, a United Nations Messenger of Peace, has advocated an end to the prolonged conflict in Darfur and greater humanitarian assistance for the area.

Carter was then in the Middle East, where he had met exiled Hamas militant leader Khalid Meshaal. Carter described his trip as a “study mission” intended to advance peace, democracy, and human rights in the region.

“MEND is prepared for talks and will prefer Ex President Jimmy Carter to mediate,” the organization wrote. “Mr. Carter is not in denial as the rest of you who brand freedom fighters as terrorists.”

The letter also warned Bush that the consequences of the pipeline attack would affect the U.S. economy and its citizens in some form, adding that MEND hoped it had now gained his attention.

The group further said the operation was retaliation for the arrest of member Henry Okah. He was detained the previous year and, according to local media reports, faced treason charges.

Since the end of 2005, MEND fighters have repeatedly struck Nigeria’s petroleum industry and kidnapped dozens of foreign employees. Nearly every captive was later freed without injury. The organization has previously said it intensified its campaign to correct what it considers an unfair division of Nigeria’s oil revenues.

The Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta (MEND), one of Nigeria’s most prominent rebel groups, said it had attacked two oil pipelines in the Niger Delta. The group described the sabotage as part of its campaign against what it considers the exploitation and neglect of the oil-producing region, where many communities remain impoverished despite decades of petroleum production.

MEND also called for international mediation to help resolve the conflict. It urged former U.S. presidents George W. Bush and Jimmy Carter, as well as actor and humanitarian activist George Clooney, to become involved in efforts to address the region’s political, economic, and environmental grievances.

Royal Dutch Shell confirmed that the pipelines had been damaged. The company said the resulting disruption would temporarily reduce oil shipments by approximately 169,000 barrels per day while repairs were carried out. The incident again demonstrated MEND’s ability to interfere with production in Nigeria, one of Africa’s leading oil exporters.

Repeated attacks on pipelines, production facilities, and other energy infrastructure have reduced Nigerian output and created uncertainty in international markets. Because Nigeria supplies large quantities of high-quality crude oil to global consumers, significant disruptions in the Niger Delta can tighten supplies and contribute to higher fuel prices worldwide.

## Lagos, Nigeria: A City in Motion

Lagos, Nigeria, is one of Africa’s largest and most dynamic cities. Known for its vibrant culture, bustling markets, growing technology sector, and influential entertainment industry, Lagos serves as a major economic hub for both Nigeria and West Africa.

From the busy streets of Lagos Island to the beaches along the Atlantic coast, the city offers striking contrasts. Modern office towers stand alongside historic neighborhoods, while music, fashion, art, and film reflect the creativity of its diverse population. Lagos is especially important to Nigeria’s globally recognized Afrobeats and Nollywood industries.

International media organizations such as CNN frequently feature Lagos in coverage of African business, culture, travel, and urban development. Although the city faces challenges—including traffic congestion, infrastructure pressure, and rapid population growth—Lagos remains a powerful symbol of ambition, resilience, and opportunity in Nigeria.
